snippet.title: Heads Up Action Soccer Longplay (Vectrex Game)
snippet.description:
- Heads Up Action Soccer Longplay (Vectrex Game) -

Heads Up Action Soccer is a soccer game developed and published by General Consumer Electronics for the Vectrex in 1983. Known as Soccer Football in Europe, it was a rare attempt to bring a team sport to a console whose vector display was particularly well suited to space shooters and racing games. Considering how much I enjoy both soccer games and the Vectrex, this ought to have been an appealing combination. Unfortunately, it turned out to be one of the worst soccer games I have ever played.

Each side consists of three outfield players and a goalkeeper, with the action taking place on a horizontally scrolling pitch viewed from a slightly elevated angle. You can compete against the computer at three difficulty settings or challenge another person using a second controller. Matches consist of two three-minute halves, with sudden-death extra time if the scores are level. Six minutes may not sound particularly long, but this is one game capable of making them feel considerably longer.

A dot above a player's head indicates who is under your control. In possession, the joystick determines the direction of movement and the two action buttons offer a choice between passing and shooting. When defending, those same buttons switch between outfield players or let you move the goalkeeper. Tackling involves getting close enough to take the ball rather than executing a separate tackling action.

There is a particularly strange concession to the scrolling display. Outfield teammates who disappear beyond one side of the visible screen can reappear on the other as the pitch moves. The manual actually encourages you to take this behavior into account when passing. It might solve a technical problem, but it makes the positioning of your players feel decidedly unnatural. Finding space in a soccer game ought to involve reading the movement of your teammates, not anticipating where someone is going to reappear.

The pace is dreadful. Moving the ball from one end of the pitch to the other takes far too long, and the encounters between opposing players rarely develop into anything resembling an exciting passage of play. The computer's reliance on dribbling rather than constructing attacks through passing only makes the matches more monotonous. There is very little of the movement, variety or spontaneity that makes a good soccer game so enjoyable.

Defending brings another source of frustration. Switching players is cumbersome, and the limited goalkeeper controls hardly inspire confidence. Even after making a save, the goalkeeper's automatic clearance can send the ball straight back into a dangerous area. That is an absurd way to undo the work of getting into position and preventing a goal in the first place.

The presentation is probably the most interesting aspect of the cartridge. The stick figures change size according to their position on the pitch, creating an impression of depth, and the scrolling is reasonably effective for the hardware. Unfortunately, distinguishing the teams by the brightness of their outlines is far less practical than using different shirt colors. The vector graphics look unusual, but they do not necessarily make the match easier to follow.

I would not judge a soccer game from 1983 by the standards of a modern simulation. Even a handful of players, a basic passing system and a single pitch can provide hours of entertainment if the movement and shooting feel right. International Soccer on the Commodore 64 appeared that same year and showed just how enjoyable a simplified interpretation of the sport could be.

Heads Up, on the other hand, manages to make a short soccer match feel like a chore. The sluggish action, awkward player management and bizarre positioning mechanics undermine almost everything I look for in this type of game. I have a great deal of affection for the Vectrex, but I cannot think of a good reason to return to this particular cartridge. Give me another round of Mine Storm instead.

#retrogamingloft #headsupactionsoccer #vectrex
